title: Public Adjuster for Roof Claim: Galveston Wind and Hail Help
description: When to hire a public adjuster for a roof claim in Galveston, how coastal wind and hail roof claims are documented, and common TWIA roof claim disputes.
html:
Roofs take the first hit from every Gulf storm, and on Galveston Island that means roof claims are among the most common and most disputed property claims we see. If your insurer has offered a small repair when you believe the roof needs replacement, or has blamed the damage on age, hiring a public adjuster for roof claim help can level the field. This article explains how coastal wind and hail roof claims work, what insurers look for, where disputes come from, and how a public adjuster fits in.

Why Coastal Roof Claims Get Disputed

A roof claim on the Texas coast usually comes down to a few questions:

  • Was the damage caused by a storm, or by age and wear? Insurers often point to granule loss, blistering, or old repairs and call it deterioration.
  • How much of the roof is damaged? The carrier may approve a few shingles or one slope, while you believe the whole system is compromised.
  • Can the roof be repaired? Brittle shingles, discontinued products, and code requirements can make spot repairs impractical.
  • What does a code-compliant repair cost? On the coast, the repair must meet windstorm requirements and may need certification.

Each of these is a factual question, and facts can be documented.

What Wind Damage to a Roof Looks Like

Wind damage is not always dramatic. Missing shingles are obvious, but many damaged shingles stay on the roof. Signs include:

  • Creased shingles, where a tab was lifted and folded back, leaving a horizontal line
  • Broken or unsealed seal strips, so tabs lift easily by hand
  • Missing or displaced ridge caps and hip caps
  • Lifted or torn flashing at walls, chimneys, and vents
  • Exposed or backed-out nails
  • Displaced metal panels or loosened fasteners on metal roofs
  • Interior leaks and attic staining after the storm

Hail on the coast is less common than inland, but it happens. Hail can leave bruises, fractured mats, and dents in vents, gutters and metal components.

Shingles are sold with manufacturer wind ratings, and a storm that exceeded those ratings is strong context for your claim. Our shingle wind damage calculator compares common shingle ratings from major manufacturers with wind speeds, and our weather events log tracks local high-wind events.

How to Document a Roof Claim Step by Step

  1. Record the storm date. Note when the wind or hail hit your area. For TWIA policies, claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss.
  2. Photograph from the ground first. Take wide shots of every slope, the yard, and any debris. Do not climb a damaged roof yourself.
  3. Document the inside. Photograph ceiling stains, wet insulation, and attic decking, with dates.
  4. Make temporary repairs. Tarp or seal openings to prevent further damage and keep every receipt. Policies expect reasonable steps to protect the property.
  5. Gather roof history. Find the installation date, product type, invoices, and any windstorm certificate for the existing roof.
  6. Get a qualified inspection. A detailed roof inspection with marked, photographed damage by slope is far more persuasive than a general statement that the roof is damaged.
  7. Report the claim and request the policy. Get your claim number and a certified copy of the policy.

When to Hire a Public Adjuster for Roof Claim Disputes

Not every roof claim needs outside help. A small, clearly covered repair may be handled well on your own. Consider hiring a public adjuster for roof claim situations like these:

  • The insurer approved spot repairs, but your roofer says the roof cannot be repaired properly
  • The claim was denied as wear and tear, age, or improper installation
  • The adjuster's estimate leaves out underlayment, flashing, drip edge, decking, or code upgrades
  • There is interior damage from leaks that was not included
  • Your home has wind and flood damage from the same storm and the carriers point at each other
  • The claim is large and you do not have time to manage the paperwork

Common Roof Claim Issues on Galveston Island

Repair versus replacement

Older asphalt shingles can become brittle, and lifting them to repair a few damaged ones may break surrounding shingles. A brittleness test and photographs can support the argument that a spot repair is not practical. Matching is another issue: if the original shingle is discontinued, a repair may leave a mismatched patch. How matching is handled depends on your policy language.

Code and certification costs

In the catastrophe area, roof replacements and many repairs must meet the windstorm building code and generally require a WPI-8 or WPI-8-C certificate. That can mean upgraded nailing patterns, deck re-nailing, specific underlayment, and engineer fees. Whether the policy pays for these depends on its terms, including any ordinance or law coverage. Our Galveston local code page explains the requirements that often drive these costs.

Depreciation and holdback

Many policies pay actual cash value first and release recoverable depreciation after repairs are completed. Know the deadline for completing repairs and submitting invoices so you do not lose the holdback.

Deductibles

Coastal wind policies often use percentage deductibles. Make sure the correct deductible is applied, and applied correctly to the event.

How TWIA Handles Roof Claims

If TWIA is your wind insurer, your roof claim is governed by your TWIA policy and Texas Insurance Code chapter 2210, which includes specific timelines and a dispute process. Read every letter TWIA sends, note any deadlines, and respond in writing. If TWIA accepts part of the claim and rejects part, the letter should explain which items are disputed. Our TWIA claims expert page covers the TWIA process in more detail.

For non-TWIA insurers, the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act in Insurance Code chapter 542 sets deadlines for acknowledging, investigating and paying claims.

What a Public Adjuster Does on a Roof Claim

A public adjuster is licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) and represents the policyholder, not the insurer. On a roof claim, a public adjuster typically:

  • Reviews the full policy, including endorsements and deductibles
  • Inspects and documents roof, attic, and interior damage in detail
  • Prepares a line-item estimate that reflects a code-compliant, certifiable repair
  • Presents supporting evidence such as weather data, brittleness tests, and product ratings
  • Handles communication and re-inspections with the insurer
  • Tracks deadlines, including depreciation recovery

A public adjuster cannot guarantee any result, and you should be wary of anyone who does. What a good public adjuster offers is a complete, organized claim that is harder to underpay.

Roof Claim Checklist

  • Storm date recorded and claim reported
  • Ground-level and interior photos taken
  • Temporary repairs made, receipts kept
  • Roof age, product, and prior certificates gathered
  • Detailed inspection with slope-by-slope documentation
  • Insurer's estimate compared line by line with a code-compliant scope
  • Depreciation and repair deadlines on the calendar

If your roof claim was denied, underpaid, or stuck, a public adjuster for roof claim support can review it with you at no cost. faq.q: When should I hire a public adjuster for a roof claim?
faq.a: Consider it when the insurer approves only spot repairs your roofer says will not work, denies the claim as wear and tear, leaves out code or interior items, or when the claim is large or complicated by both wind and flood damage.

faq.q: Does my insurer have to pay for a full roof replacement?
faq.a: It depends on the extent of storm damage, whether a proper repair is possible, and your policy terms, including any matching and ordinance or law provisions. Detailed documentation of the damage and repair limits is key.

faq.q: How long do I have to report a TWIA roof claim?
faq.a: TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss. Reporting sooner is better, because evidence of storm damage is easier to document right after the event.
